doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Monitors and acoustic sound in clubs
summary: Too many monitors hurt acoustic music; last night's club sound improved by stripping amplification.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, a mistake is one thing. But this was like a collision. And you know, what does that mean? It’s a big stage with too many monitors. So you can’t hear anything, to me. I mean this music is acoustic music. The more monitors they put up there the less you can hear.
Because they probably couldn’t hear it. “Give me more me in the monitors.” “No, give me more of them” except for me, I need to hear me or else I’m going to sing in a different key.
Yeah I know what you mean. Like you can hear everything and nothing. It’s like loud but you can’t hear. It’s a very weird situation that we find ourselves in often. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Last night the sound was fantastic in the club. We started out with acoustic piano, an upright. The piano was miced. There were a couple of monitors and I think the bass was in one of the monitors, and so was I. It’s a little room. You know how it ended up? Acoustic piano with the top taken off. You know it’s an upright so they took the top off. And take the mic off the bass and have him come through his amp. The drummer played mostly brushes. Now I don’t have to holler. So we could all hear, they can hear, you hear all the nuances. You know it’s not rock & roll. We’re not trying to fill a stadium.
Right. And people listen more intently if they’re not being —
Yeah. If their hair’s not moving.
